lay_term: The antibiotic tetracycline works in the body to fight bacteria. A provider uses this code to report one unit of this code for up to 250 mg of tetracycline.ExplanationTetracycline is an antibiotic that treats a wide variety of bacterial infections. Examples of typical conditions where a provider will administer this drug to a patient include urinary tract infections, acne, and certain sexually transmitted diseases such as syphilis. The provider reports this code the supply of up to 250 mg of tetracycline administered to a patient by injection. This code represents only the drug, and not the administration of the drug.TerminologyAcne: Eruptions of small oil–secreting glands below the skin surface due to infection or inflammation; also known as pimples. Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits infection. Bacteria: Single–celled microorganisms visible only with a microscope, some of which cause infection. Infection: A disease condition that bacteria, viruses, or other microorganisms cause. Injection: Use of a syringe to forcibly instill a liquid substance into tissues or vessels. mg: Abbreviation for milligram, 1/1000 of a gram (g); a metric measurement for mass or weight. Syphilis: A sexually transmitted disease (STD), that results from infection with the bacterium Treponema pallidum; primary and secondary stages occur early in the disease; latent syphilis may develop many years later and affect multiple organ systems and lead to death; an infected mother can pass the infection to her baby in the womb. One unit of this code represents 1 mg of omadacycline, a tetracycline–class antibiotic, administered by intravenous infusion to treat community–acquired bacterial pneumonia and acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections.ExplanationThe recommended dosage of omadacycline is an intravenous infusion of 200 mg over a 60–minute period once or 100 mg over a 30–minute period twice on day one, followed by a maintenance daily dose of 100 mg over a 30–minute period for 7 to 14 days. Omadacycline is supplied as 100 mg of omadacycline (equivalent to 131 mg omadacycline tosylate) as a lyophilized (freeze–dried) powder in a single–dose vial to be reconstituted and further diluted before being administered. Report this code for each 1 mg of omadacycline administered. Omadacycline is used to treat community–acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP) and acute bacterial skin and skin structure infection (ABSSSI). CABP is a common lung infection acquired outside of a hospital setting, i.e., in the community, caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae bacteria and atypical bacteria such as Chlamydia pneumoniae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Legionella species. ABSSSI refers to serious bacterial skin infections, including cellulitis, erysipelas, wound infections, and major skin abscesses, covering a surface area of approximately 75 sq cm. Common bacterial pathogens that cause ABSSSI are Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus including methicillin–resistant S. aureus (MRSA). To prevent drug resistance, culture and sensitivity should be performed prior to administering omadacycline.TerminologyAbscess: A collection of pus in a walled–off sac or pocket, the result of infection. Antibiotic: Substance that inhibits or treats bacterial infections. Erysipelas: A bacterial skin infection that involves the upper layer of skin (dermis) and superficial cutaneous lymphatics; it is characterized by well–defined margins, severe inflammation and redness, and hardened skin patches. Intravenous (IV) infusion: The administration of medication, fluid, electrolytes, and/or nutrition to a patient through a catheter into a vein when the patient cannot take these treatments orally or because of the need for an immediate response; infusion therapy is usually gradual and measured, taking place over a period of time from minutes to hours to days. mg: Abbreviation for milligram, 1/1000 of a gram (g); a metric measurement for mass or weight. Pneumonia: An inflammation or swelling of the lungs accompanied by high fever, followed by consolidation (solidification or hardening) of the lungs with filling of the lungs with fluid; this condition slowly resolves, and the lungs slowly clear up as the infection subsides. sq cm, cm2: Abbreviation for square centimeter, a metric unit of measure of area; in cm2, the 2 is usually superscripted; 1 cm equals approximately 0.39 inches, or just over a third of an inch, so a square centimeter would be 1 cm x 1 cm.TipsThis is a generic drug. Brand names for this drug include Nuzyra®. This code represents the supply of the drug. lay_term: This manmade protein, abatacept, works in the body to prevent the body’s immune system from harming its own tissues such as joints. A provider uses this code to report one unit of 10 mg of abatacept. Routes of administration include subcutaneous injection. Use this code only when the provider supervises the administration of the drug.ExplanationAbatacept is a manmade protein that stops the body’s own immune response from attacking the healthy tissues of a patient such as the patient’s joints. The drug is intended for children, ages 2–17 years of age, with moderate to severe polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Report this code for the supply of each 10 mg of abatacept by subcutaneous injection, when administered by the provider. The recommended dosage is based on the patient's weight. For patients weighing 10 mg to less than 25 mg, the recommended dosage is 50 mg in 0.4 mL preservative–free solution (PFS), for patients weighing 25 kg up to 50 kg, 87.5 mg (0.7 mL PFS), and for patients weighing over 50 kg, 125 (1 mL PFS). This code may not be reported if the patient self–administers the drug. This code represents only the supply of the drug, not the administration of the drug.TerminologyAutoimmune: Response of the immune system against own body. Idiopathic: Unknown origin or cause. Immune response: The actions of the body to protect itself against potentially harmful substances, such as bacteria, viruses, toxins, and foreign objects, including transplanted organs. Joint: Point of union of two musculoskeletal structures, such as two bones. mg: Abbreviation for milligram, 1/1000 of a gram (g); a metric measurement for mass or weight. mL: Abbreviation for milliliter, a metric measurement for volume; 1 mL equals approximately 0.034 U.S. fluid ounces; previously known as a cubic centimeter (cc). Polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis: Swelling and inflammation of joints in children 16 years of age or younger. Subcutaneous injection: Injecting small amounts of medications or other liquids in the fatty layer below the skin, sometimes shortened to subcu injection. Vein: A blood vessel that carries the deoxygenated blood in the body.TipsThis is a generic drug. Brand names for this drug include Orencia®. This code represents the supply of the drug. This anticlotting agent, abciximab, works in the body to prevent platelets from sticking together and forming clots. This code represents one unit of 10 mg of abciximab. Routes of administration include intravenous injection or infusion.ExplanationAbciximab is a monoclonal antibody anticlotting agent that prevents the platelets in a patient’s body from sticking together and forming clots. This drug prevents cardiac complications during percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) procedures. The provider reports this code for the supply of 10 mg of abciximab for bolus injection or intravenous infusion. Abciximab is supplied as a 2 mg/mL solution. The recommended dosage is based on weight and is 0.25 mg/kg by bolus injection over one minute 10 minutes to one hour before the start of a percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) procedure, then 0.125 mcg/kg per minute by IV continuous infusion for 12 hours, not to exceed an infusion rate of 10 mcg per minute. For patients with unstable angina within 24 hours of a planned PCI procedure, the dosages are the same, but the continuous infusion lasts for 18–24 hours and ends one hour post–PCI. This code represents only the supply of the drug and not the administration of the drug.TerminologyAngina: Pain in the chest when the heart is not receiving sufficient oxygen. Artery: A blood vessel carrying blood away from the heart to an organ or body part. Bolus: A relatively large dose of a therapeutic or diagnostic substance administered intravenously over a short period of time. Cardiac: Of the heart. Coronary: Refers to the blood vessels that supply the muscles and walls of the heart. Monoclonal antibody: A protein, made in a laboratory, that can identify and bind itself to a particular type of cell in order to block its function or to carry medicine or radioactive substances directly to it. Percutaneous: Literally, through the skin. Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI): A minimally invasive surgical procedure to treat diseased heart vessels using a catheter inserted through the skin of the groin and into a vessel; the catheter is advanced to the heart, and various instruments inserted through it to treat stricture (narrowing) or remove plaque. Platelets: A component of blood that helps in clotting. Vein: A blood vessel that carries the deoxygenated blood in the body.TipsThis is a generic drug. Brand names for this drug include: ReoPro®. The provider reports this code for the supply of 100 mg of acetylcysteine administered by intravenous injection. This code represents only the supply of the drug and not the administration of the drug.TerminologyAcetaminophen: A drug similar to aspirin to treat mild to moderate pain and fever; unlike aspirin, acetaminophen's anti–inflammatory properties are weak; chronic or excessive use can be toxic to the liver; a popular brand name for acetaminophen is Tylenol. Cold sores: An infection due to herpes simplex virus that causes blisters around the mouth and lips, which heal slowly by 2 to 3 weeks; also known as herpes labialis, fever blisters, or orolabial herpes. Herpes: A painful, localized skin rash of blister–like eruptions that results from activation of the herpes virus, the virus that also causes chickenpox; also known as herpes zoster and shingles. Crohn’s disease is a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) that causes inflammation in the digestive tract. Ulcerative colitis is another form of IBD that causes inflammation and ulcers in the inner lining of the large intestine (colon) and rectum. short_description: Riboflavin 5’-phosphate, ophthalmic solution, up to 3 ml

short_description: Prothrombin complex concentrate (human), kcentra, per i.u. of factor ix activity

Providers typically administer it intravenously in a patient who requires reversal of blood thinner therapy because of acute major bleeding or the need for urgent surgery.ExplanationThe dosage of Kcentra® is determined by the patient’s pretreatment INR and body weight. Typical dosage may range from 25 IU/kg to 50 IU/kg. Administration is by intravenous infusion. Kcentra® is supplied as single–use vials with a range of 400–620 factor IX units per vial or 800–1240 units per vial. Providers may administer Kcentra® to reverse the effect of anticoagulation (blood thinner) therapy in a patient with major bleeding or who needs urgent surgery. Anticoagulants like warfarin that are vitamin–K antagonists (VKA) work by disrupting the role of vitamin K in a complex series of events that cause blood clotting. Kcentra® increases levels of the vitamin K–dependent coagulation factors that VKAs deplete. This prothrombin (clotting factor) complex concentrate (PCC) includes all four vitamin–K dependent coagulation factors (II, VII, IX, and X) as well as the natural coagulation inhibitors protein C and protein S. One unit of this code represents 1 mg of live BCG instilled into the bladder (intravesically) to treat bladder cancer.ExplanationThe recommended dose of TheraCys® is one 81 mg vial of reconstituted freeze–dried BCG supplied in a single vial. Maintenance therapy for TheraCys® is one dose at 3, 6, 12, 18 and 24 months following the initial dose; for TICE®, the recommended maintenance dose is once monthly after the initial six weeks for up to 12 months. After the first 15 minutes of lying prone (on the back), the patient should turn to the side, then onto the stomach, then the other side, and back to the back every 15 minutes to ensure that all bladder surfaces are treated. The patient should also stand if able at least once before the treatment is completed. lay_term: This code represents 1 mg daunorubicin and 2.27 mg cytarabine liposome administered by intravenous injection to treat newly diagnosed, therapy–related acute myeloid leukemia (t–AML) or AML with myelodysplasia–related changes in adults.ExplanationThe usual induction dosage is daunorubicin 44 mg/m2 and cytarabine 100 mg/m2 liposome by intravenous infusion over a 90–minute period on days 1, 3, and 5, and on days 1 and 3 of subsequent cycles, if needed. A second induction cycle 2 to 5 weeks after the first may be administered for patients who fail to achieve remission after the first induction cycle, if there was no unacceptable toxicity. Five to 8 weeks after the start of the last induction, a consolidation cycle consisting of daunorubicin 29 mg/m2 and cytarabine 65 mg/m2 over a 90–minute period on days 1 and 3 is recommended for patients who do not show disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. A full course consists of 1 to 2 cycles of induction (the second cycle only for patients failing to achieve a response from the first induction) followed by up to 2 cycles of consolidation. It is supplied in single–dose glass vial of 44 mg daunorubicin and 100 mg cytarabine encapsulated in liposomes in a freeze–dried cake for reconstitution. Myeloid leukemia occurs when myeloblasts (immature blood cells in the bone marrow) enter the blood stream or when the bone marrow (the spongy tissue inside large bones) produces abnormal white blood cells which then overwhelm or replace healthy blood cells and keep the blood from functioning as it should. Patients tend to bruise or bleed easily and suffer from fever, fatigue, difficulty breathing, loss of appetite with weight loss, and weakness.TerminologyAcute: Refers to a disease or an ailment that has rapid onset or short course.
